pr_title: Use IndexOfAnyValues in the RegexCompiler and source gen
pr_body:
Closes #78203

For the source generator, we emit `IndexOfAnyValues` definitions under `Utilities`
```c#
file static class Utilities
{
    internal static readonly IndexOfAnyValues<char> AsciiHexDigit =
        IndexOfAnyValues.Create("0123456789ABCDEFabcdef");

    internal static readonly IndexOfAnyValues<char> Ascii_800600008006 =
        IndexOfAnyValues.Create("WYZwyz");
}
```
Whereas for the RegexCompiler, I added a new `IndexOfAnyValues<char>[]` field to `CompiledRegexRunner` and the callers end up looking something like
```c#
span.IndexOfAny(this._indexOfAnyValues[42]);
```

---

A few issues I came across while working on this:
- Sets of 3-5 values that fall in a single range should likely prefer using the range
  - Sets like "abcd" now turn into `IndexOfAnyValues` instead of `InRange('a', 'd')`
- The `Chars` for the `FixedDistanceSet` optimization don't support negated sets
  - Sets like `[^ab]` now end up using `IndexOfAnyValues` instead of `IndexOfAnyExcept('a', 'b')`
  - The number of places using `IndexOfAnyValues` is probably inflated because of this

---

@stephentoub Can you please take a look at this to see if it makes any sense?
The tests are passing, but I don't have in-depth knowledge about all the tradeoffs being made in Regex.

How do you go about benchmarking a change like this? Just pick a few patterns that you know will be affected?

Author: MihaZupan
Assignees: MihaZupan
Labels: `area-System.Text.RegularExpressions`
Milestone: 8.0.0

> Sets of 3-5 values that fall in a single range should likely prefer using the range

Is this something you plan to address in this PR, or we should address it subsequently?

> The Chars for the FixedDistanceSet optimization don't support negated sets

Probably worth opening an issue for this.  That said, I've seen diminishing returns in the past around the negated sets, as it's often (not always) the case that the thing you're then searching for occurs really soon.

> Can you please take a look at this to see if it makes any sense?

It's lovely.  Nice work.

> The tests are passing

Can you run outerloop locally as well?  That'll run another ~18,000 patterns through the source generator and compiler.

> How do you go about benchmarking a change like this? Just pick a few patterns that you know will be affected?

For a sweeping change like this, I'll typically run all the regex tests in dotnet/performance, in particular https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/main/src/benchmarks/micro/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/Perf.Regex.Industry.cs, https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/main/src/benchmarks/micro/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/Perf.Regex.Common.cs, and https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/main/src/benchmarks/micro/runtime/BenchmarksGame/regex-redux-5.cs.

> > Sets of 3-5 values that fall in a single range should likely prefer using the range

> Is this something you plan to address in this PR, or we should address it subsequently?

Experimenting with it locally the diff is racking up LOC, so I'll follow up with a second PR.

|              Method |         Toolchain |              Options |          Mean |        Error | Ratio | MannWhitney(5%) |
|-------------------- |------------------ |--------------------- |--------------:|-------------:|------:|---------------- |
| OneNodeBacktracking | \main\corerun.exe | IgnoreCase, Compiled |      58.89 ns |     0.370 ns |  1.00 |            Base |
| OneNodeBacktracking |   \pr\corerun.exe | IgnoreCase, Compiled |      77.09 ns |     0.458 ns |  1.31 |          Slower |

Cases like [`OneNodeBacktracking`](https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/ddb274bb2764a4c524e77499c30d3c3bbe0b59d8/src/benchmarks/micro/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/Perf.Regex.Common.cs#L41) (`[^a]+\.[^z]+`) regress for `IgnoreCase + Compiled` where it starts using `IndexOfAnyExcept(this._array[42])`.

I'd have to check what this means for source-generated cases where there's less per-call overhead for `IndexOfAnyValues` compared to the compiled version.

I'll keep digging...

- I did make the "prefer the range over chars for sets like `[abc]`" here.
- I also removed the negated `AsciiSet` variant from the primary set as it only seemed to have regressed things.
   - I had the change to allow negated sets of 2-5 chars as well, but the benchmarks weren't happy. I'll open an issue to track that.
- The only negated primary set is the range (as before this PR), I just made a change to use `IndexOfAnyExcept('a')` instead of `IndexOfAnyExceptInRange('a', 'a')` for length=1 sets.
- I tweaked the primary set sorting again as my change to check the length of chars first regressed some patterns by preferring things like `IndexOf(' ')` over `IndexOfAny('k', 'K', 'K')` (where the space has a much higher frequency according to the table).

Here are all the Regex benchmarks from `dotnet/performance`: https://gist.github.com/MihaZupan/533a8b9c57815077cec768b59f17b835

The largest regression is for the `\p{Sm}` pattern when using the interpreter/NonBacktracking engine - not sure how I did that.

issue_context.title: Use new IndexOfAnyValues in RegexCompiler and source generator
issue_context.body: Once https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/78093 is merged, we'll want to use it in the RegexCompiler and source generator.  This will require reworking the heuristics for when we consider sets viable for being used with IndexOf, updating the relevant data structures to pass along the relevant info, and updating the code emitters appropriately.

Issue Details
Once https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/78093 is merged, we'll want to use it in the RegexCompiler and source generator. This will require reworking the heuristics for when we consider sets viable for being used with IndexOf, updating the relevant data structures to pass along the relevant info, and updating the code emitters appropriately.
Author: stephentoub
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Text.RegularExpressions`
Milestone: 8.0.0
I have some local experiments with this already. I'll take a crack at it and unassign myself if I fail miserably :)

review_comments: This is fine for now.  We might want to look at deduplicating (e.g. with a `Dictionary<string, (int, IndexOfAnyValues<char>)>` instead of a `List<IndexOfAnyValues<char>>`) when the same character class is used multiple times in the pattern, as that's relatively common.
Can you run the FunctionalTests with /p:Coverage=true and make sure all the new code paths are covered (and if not, add tests to ensure they are)?

The `TryFindNextStartingPositionLeftToRight` and `TryFindNextStartingPositionRightToLeft` in [RegexFindOptimizations.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexFindOptimizations.cs#L438) are never hit, both before and after my change.

I'm assuming these are parts of the interpreter. Am I missing some extra argument for the tests?
Nvm, I was looking at the same file but under the source generator coverage 🤦‍♂️

The only places I see missing any coverage are the negated Chars FixedDistanceSets in `SortFixedDistanceSetsByQuality`.

Specifically
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/981d33c2ae465f9156f85817763d3926f5c6f3a7/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexPrefixAnalyzer.cs#L457-L465
And
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/981d33c2ae465f9156f85817763d3926f5c6f3a7/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/RegexPrefixAnalyzer.cs#L471-L474

I failed to come up with a pattern that would hit those paths (presumably it should contain multiple length=1 negated `FixedDistanceSet`s).
Any tips on what those might look like appreciated :)

That's building up a list of all possible characters that could occur at a specific distance from the start of the pattern.  Alternations are your best bet.  So, for example, if you have the pattern:
```
Steve|Miha
```
that's going to generate the sets:
```
[SM]
[ti]
[eh]
[va]
```
or if you have:
```
[0-9][a-z]|[A-Z]7
```
that'll generate the sets:
```
[0-9A-Z]
[a-z7]
```
Oh, wait, those are for negated-related checks. The existing code isn't capable of producing negated sets, at least as far as I remember... does this PR change that?

The most I could get it to do was a single length=1 negated set (e.g. literally `[^a]`) which is likely coming from the `FindFirstCharClass` fallback if we found nothing useful.

It does produce negated sets for patterns like `[a-q][^u-z]{13}x` that will turn into
`[a-q], [^u-z], [^u-z], [^u-z], [^u-z], [^u-z], ...`
I just wasn't sure if it's possible for length=1 sets as well.

This PR doesn't affect the kinds of sets we initially produce, but it will change sets that would previously become `Range` with `low==high` into Length=1 `Chars`.
I initially did this to use `Chars` for length 1-5 negated sets instead of `IndexOfAnyValues`, but since then I've reverted the negated `IndexOfAnyValues` from this path. Now some of this new logic is useless and it should just defer to `Range` (which has low==high special-cased already), I'll clean this up.
Removed the unnecessary logic I introduced with this PR, code coverage now looks good.
Moving this is fine, but I'm curious, is this just style or did something cause there to start being a warning on that existing field as well?

I think I just expected that a similar warning would fire for the new field, but I see now that `_caseBehavior` is the only one not set by the ctor ... I don't remember why I moved the culture as well.

I suppose neither `_indexOfAnyValues` nor `_culture` actually need to be in the pragma.
